answer.rationale: The binding constraints eliminate most options before verification. negotiate_terms is already foreclosed eopen price this cycley: the contract does not auto-renew, so letting it lapse at 94% utilization with no buffer creates an unsupplied line, not budget flexibility (memory_c5 applied to a non-critical, month-to-month-eligible service, which this is not). memory_c6's multi-year volume pricing and memory_c4's benchmarking leverage both require a willing counterparty. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the strongest risk story but does not resolve the expiring primary award and captures only a fraction of an 18% mandate. That leaves the low-cost vendor, which is exactly why memory_c2 is the one record worth the verification budget: it is the sole basis for believing that vendor can carry primary volume, and as consolidated it is conspicuously narrow. It attests to unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy \u2014 all commercial and back-office attributes \u2014 and is silent on on-time delivery, fill rate, and behavior at committed volume, which are the only attributes that matter given zero buffer. It also says 'last year' at an unstated volume that may have been a trial rather than full primary load. Cost performance has been carried forward as if it were reliability performance; that substitution is the drift I want the archived record to confirm or refute. So: award primary to the low-cost vendor, but as a guarded staged ramp \u2014 a bounded initial share with the incumbent's current lot flow held as fallback and explicit fill-rate gates before each volume increment. This captures the mandate's trajectory while keeping the line covered if memory_c2 turns out to document a cheap supplier rather than a dependable one. If the archived record shows the prior engagement was low-volume or lacks delivery data, I downgrade to add_second_source at the same guarded scale and treat the mandate as a two-cycle target rather than forcing it in 14 days.
